title: Good King Wenceslas
description: John Mason Neale's carol of the good king and his page, to the old tune Thomas Helmore set it to in Carols for Christmas-tide, for 2 to 4 singers: the first verse, the page and the king in the snow (verse 4) and the last verse's blessing, steady and bright in A major. The alto moves in thirds and sixths under the tune, and each verse's last line comes home over a held A in the bass.

credits.tune: "Tempus adest floridum" (Piae Cantiones, 1582), as Thomas Helmore set it to Neale's words
credits.arrangement: Stackapella, on the chords of Bramley and Stainer's Christmas Carols New and Old

licence.words: public domain: John Mason Neale died 1866
licence.tune: public domain: the spring carol "Tempus adest floridum" (Piae Cantiones, 1582), as Thomas Helmore (died 1890) set it to Neale's words in Carols for Christmas-tide; Bramley and Stainer print the same tune
licence.arrangement: original, written for Stackapella: our own alto, tenor and bass under the tune as Neale and Helmore print it. The chords follow the four-part harmony of Bramley and Stainer's Christmas Carols New and Old, which is unsigned (the book's editors: John Stainer, died 1901, and Henry Ramsden Bramley, died 1917), so it was used only to check which chords are right, never copied part by part; Helmore's own harmony in the 1854 condensed vocal parts, a different setting, was compared where the scan is legible. Our chords are theirs beat by beat in every verse, except: a seventh (D) is added to the E chords at beats 3 and 35 (alto, tenor) and left out at 43; "a" in "When a poor man" (49) is A over A, not over C-sharp, so the alto and bass don't move in octaves; and under the tune's two-note "fu-" (60) every lower part holds one note for the syllable, the bass on A, so F-sharp minor and D (they print F-sharp and D in the bass) become F-sharp minor and D over a held A and the line closes plagally on the tonic. One note a syllable in every lower part; the alto takes the chord's third wherever the tune hasn't it on every strong beat, so the duet and trio are complete harmony there; on a few weak beats (3, 5, 9, 41 and 59 of each verse) the duet or trio passes without the third, each forced by the voice-leading or the beginner ranges; breaths written in for beginners (each line's last note gives up a beat). Beats are each verse's own, from 0. Accepted exceptions: the alto leaps G#4, a beat's rest and breath, then C#4 to F#4 at the start of "came in sight"'s next line (beat 57 of each verse), each note the only one that keeps the duet's third; the soprano and alto sit more than an octave apart, E5 over C#4, at beats 32 and 56 of each verse, forced by the duet (A4 would be a bare fourth, E4 a bare octave, C#5 above the alto's range); and the soprano and tenor move in fifths from 54 to 56 across the rest and the breath, where every other tenor note is worse.
licence.source: The Condensed Vocal Parts to the Carols for Christmas-tide; set to Ancient Melodies by the Rev. T. Helmore, M.A.; the Words, principally in imitation of the original, by the Rev. J. M. Neale, M.A. (London: J. Alfred Novello, 1854), No. XI, "Good King Wenceslas", pp. 37 to 40, in four parts on two staves in A major, common time, every verse under the music, written here in A as printed; the tune and verses 1, 4 and 5 as printed there, the long s modernised, and the opening quotation mark it prints at the start of each line of speech kept only where each speech begins (its single closing mark after "longer" written as a double one); read from the scan at commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:The_Condensed_Vocal_Parts_to_the_Carols_for_Christmas-tide.pdf (a Google scan of HathiTrust record 011630024), PDF pages 43 to 46. The chords checked against H. R. Bramley and John Stainer, Christmas Carols New and Old, first series (London: Novello, Ewer and Co.; this copy a printing of the 1870s, catalogued [187?]), No. X, "Good King Wenceslas", pp. 20 and 21, in four parts in A major, the same tune; University of California Libraries copy, archive.org/details/christmascarolsn00staiiala/page/n25 (music), n26 (verses) and n51 (index). Its words differ in small ways ("Stephen,", "crisp and even", "Mark my footsteps, my good page", "saint", "Therefore Christian men"); the first printing's are kept, "good my page" as it is sung today; the earliest known printing is the folio Carols for Christmas-tide, out by 28 October 1853, the date of the 1854 book's Notice, which refers to it (Wikimedia Commons PDF, p. 10)
